\chapter{Espanol, and Your First Built Sentence}
\label{ch:spanish-espanol}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the language and build a whole sentence from parts I chose myself.}

Hispania to espanol, and the first sentence assembled rather than memorised.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[español]{español — the word for the language}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-espanol}



\begin{quote}
You have practised writing this word's \textbf{ñ}. Now find out what is inside it — because \emph{español} is not a Spanish-made word at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{español} = \textquotedblleft{}Spanish\textquotedblright{} — both the language and a Spaniard — from \textbf{Hispania}, the \textbf{Roman} name for the Iberian peninsula. The path \emph{Hispania $\to$ hispaniolus $\to$ español} wore the word down, and there is the \textbf{ñ} again, exactly the \emph{-ni-} squeeze you met in the writing lesson (\emph{Hispaniolus} $\to$ \emph{españ-ol}). Say it \emph{es-pa-\textbf{NYOL}}.

Two footnotes worth having:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item English \textbf{Spanish}, \textbf{Hispanic} and \textbf{Hispania} are all the same root, so the English and Spanish names for the language are cousins, not translations of each other.
  \item \emph{Hispania} itself may go back through Latin to a \textbf{Phoenician} name for the coast, often read as \textquotedblleft{}land of hyraxes\textquotedblright{} (or rabbits) — the Phoenicians having met an unfamiliar animal and reached for the nearest word they had.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}español\textquotedblright{} — \emph{es-pa-NYOL}
  \item the path — \textquotedblleft{}Hispania, hispaniolus, español\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}español\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}Hispanic\textquotedblright{} — same root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{español} come from? (\textbf{Hispania}, the Roman name for Iberia.) What letter does its ending bring back, and from what Latin sequence? (\textbf{ñ}, from \textbf{-ni-} in \emph{Hispaniolus}.) Next: put it behind a verb and build your first sentence.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Hablo español]{Hablo español — your first real sentence}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-hablo-espanol}



\begin{quote}
This is the moment this book has been building to. You take a \textbf{verb} you conjugated yourself and a \textbf{noun} you took apart yourself, and make a sentence \textbf{nobody handed you pre-assembled}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the sentence assembled}]
Snap two things you already own together:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Hablo} (I speak, from \emph{hablar}) + \textbf{español} (Spanish) = \textbf{Hablo español.}
\end{quote}

That is a complete, grammatical Spanish sentence, and notice what is \textbf{not} in it: no separate subject word. The \emph{-o} of \emph{hablo} already says \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — the pro-drop you just learned, doing real work in a real sentence.

Now swap the pieces and watch it generate:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Estudio español.} — \textquotedblleft{}I study Spanish.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{Trabajo.} — \textquotedblleft{}I work.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{¿Hablas español?} — \textquotedblleft{}Do you speak Spanish?\textquotedblright{} (the \textbf{¿ ?} pair opening and closing the question, as in the writing lesson).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: languages go bare}]
One more thing missing from \emph{hablo español}: \textbf{no \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} no \textquotedblleft{}a.\textquotedblright{}} After a verb like \emph{hablar} or \emph{estudiar}, a language name takes \textbf{no article} — \emph{hablo español}, never \emph{hablo el español}.

This matters because Spanish otherwise loves its articles far more than English does (\emph{me gusta \textbf{el} café}, \textquotedblleft{}I like coffee\textquotedblright{}). So this is a genuine exception you have to hold onto, and the rule of thumb is narrow: right after \emph{hablar}, the language goes bare.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Hablo español\textquotedblright{} — \emph{AH-bloh es-pa-NYOL}
  \item swap the verb — \textquotedblleft{}Estudio español\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Trabajo\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask it — \textquotedblleft{}¿Hablas español?\textquotedblright{} (raise the pitch; ¿ opens it)
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
You met \textbf{no} long ago as the answer. It has a second job, and now you have a sentence to try it on: put \emph{no} directly in front of the verb and the whole thing flips.

\textbf{Hablo español} $\to$ \textbf{No hablo español.}

That is all there is to it. English needs a helper — \emph{do not} — and Spanish needs nothing: one small word, in front, and the sentence means its opposite.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak Spanish,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}I study Spanish.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablo español; estudio español}.) Why is there no separate subject word? (The \emph{-o} ending carries \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{}) Why no \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} before \emph{español}? (\textbf{Languages take no article} after a verb like \emph{hablar}.) You just built a sentence from parts — that is the whole game from here.
\end{tcolorbox}
